# H-2 — CSE-CIC-IDS2018 Backup Dataset Verification

*SentinelAI · Data & Features (Habiba) · generated by `h2_make_report.py` from the evidence files in `h2_outputs/`. Verified = checked by our own code on the real files; Documented = stated by an official or published source and not re-checked by us.*

**Decision: Suitable with conditions** — as a backup for the Random Forest detection part (objective O1), not as a drop-in replacement for the whole SentinelAI pipeline. See section 9.

## 1. Objective and link to H-1

Tracker task H-2: check the CSE-CIC-IDS2018 backup (size, format, labels). Done when there is a short note on how to switch if AIT fails the gate. H-1 gave AIT a conditional GO, so this backup is not needed now. H-2 makes sure the team knows, with evidence, what switching would involve and cost.

## 2. Official source (Documented)

- Official page: Canadian Institute for Cybersecurity, University of New Brunswick — https://www.unb.ca/cic/datasets/ids-2018.html (collaboration between the Communications Security Establishment and CIC).
- Official download: public AWS bucket `s3://cse-cic-ids2018/` (region ca-central-1), AWS Open Data registry https://registry.opendata.aws/cse-cic-ids2018/. No account is needed. The page asks users to cite the dataset and link the registry page.
- Paper: I. Sharafaldin, A. H. Lashkari, A. A. Ghorbani, *Toward Generating a New Intrusion Detection Dataset and Intrusion Traffic Characterization*, ICISSP 2018.
- Purpose: a benchmark for network intrusion detection, built from benign user profiles and attack profiles. Seven attack scenarios (brute force, Heartbleed, botnet, DoS, DDoS, web attacks, infiltration) were run by 50 attacker machines against an organisation of 5 departments, 420 machines and 30 servers. Flow features were extracted with CICFlowMeter-V3.

## 3. Bucket structure and size (Verified)

The bucket was listed anonymously from Colab (`s3_bucket_listing.csv`): **42 objects, 452.75 GiB in total**.

| Folder | Objects (incl. folder markers) | Size | Contents |
|---|---|---|---|
| Original Network Traffic and Log data | 31 | 446.34 GiB | Per day: one PCAP archive (35.9–55.0 GiB) and one logs.zip (0.13–0.22 GiB) |
| Processed Traffic Data for ML Algorithms | 11 | 6.41 GiB | 10 CSV files, one per capture day (labelled flows) |

Only the processed CSVs are practical for SentinelAI in Colab. The raw PCAPs (hundreds of GiB) would only be needed to regenerate flows with IP addresses or corrected labels.

- **Format:** comma-separated text with one header row; one row is one bidirectional flow. 9 files share the same 80-column header. Thuesday-20-02-2018_TrafficForML_CICFlowMeter.csv has 84 columns: the extra columns are Flow ID, Src IP, Src Port, Dst IP. Shared columns are in the same order.
- **Organisation:** by day, not by attack. Each day file mixes benign traffic with that day's one or two attacks.
- **Size in practice:** the largest file is 4,055 MB with 7,948,748 rows. It fits Colab only when read in chunks.

## 5. Labels (Verified) and proposed binary mapping

The label column is `Label` in every file. The full scan found **15 distinct values** in 16,232,943 flows. Strings were compared exactly; none contain leading or trailing whitespace. 59 further rows contain the literal text `Label`: these are repeated header lines inside the data and are not flows.

CIC publishes no benign/malicious list (AIT has `label_info.txt`), so the mapping below is **proposed by H-2**. Each attack label is tied to a scenario on the official page. Only the exact string `Benign` maps to 0; any unknown value stays unmapped.

| label | attack_scenario | binary_label | flows | days | share % |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `Benign` | Normal traffic | 0 | 13,484,708 | Friday-02-03-2018, Friday-16-02-2018, Friday-23-02-2018, Thuesday-20-02-2018, Thursday-01-03-2018, Thursday-15-02-2018, Thursday-22-02-2018, Wednesday-14-02-2018, Wednesday-21-02-2018, Wednesday-28-02-2018 | 83.07 |
| `DDOS attack-HOIC` | DDoS (HOIC) - 21-02 | 1 | 686,012 | Wednesday-21-02-2018 | 4.23 |
| `DDoS attacks-LOIC-HTTP` | DDoS (LOIC-HTTP) - 20-02 | 1 | 576,191 | Thuesday-20-02-2018 | 3.55 |
| `DoS attacks-Hulk` | DoS (Hulk) - 16-02 | 1 | 461,912 | Friday-16-02-2018 | 2.85 |
| `Bot` | Botnet (Zeus, Ares) - 02-03 | 1 | 286,191 | Friday-02-03-2018 | 1.76 |
| `FTP-BruteForce` | Brute-force (FTP, Patator) - 14-02 | 1 | 193,360 | Wednesday-14-02-2018 | 1.19 |
| `SSH-Bruteforce` | Brute-force (SSH, Patator) - 14-02 | 1 | 187,589 | Wednesday-14-02-2018 | 1.16 |
| `Infilteration` | Infiltration from inside (spelling as in the data) - 28-02, 01-03 | 1 | 161,934 | Thursday-01-03-2018, Wednesday-28-02-2018 | 1.00 |
| `DoS attacks-SlowHTTPTest` | DoS (SlowHTTPTest) - 16-02 | 1 | 139,890 | Friday-16-02-2018 | 0.86 |
| `DoS attacks-GoldenEye` | DoS (GoldenEye) - 15-02 | 1 | 41,508 | Thursday-15-02-2018 | 0.26 |
| `DoS attacks-Slowloris` | DoS (Slowloris) - 15-02 | 1 | 10,990 | Thursday-15-02-2018 | 0.07 |
| `DDOS attack-LOIC-UDP` | DDoS (LOIC-UDP) - 20-02 and 21-02 | 1 | 1,730 | Wednesday-21-02-2018 | 0.01 |
| `Brute Force -Web` | Web attack: brute force - 22-02, 23-02 | 1 | 611 | Friday-23-02-2018, Thursday-22-02-2018 | 0.00 |
| `Brute Force -XSS` | Web attack: XSS - 22-02, 23-02 | 1 | 230 | Friday-23-02-2018, Thursday-22-02-2018 | 0.00 |
| `SQL Injection` | Web attack: SQL injection - 22-02, 23-02 | 1 | 87 | Friday-23-02-2018, Thursday-22-02-2018 | 0.00 |

Result: Normal (0) = **13,484,708**, Suspicious (1) = **2,748,235** (16.93%), unmapped = **0**.

**Label consistency (Verified):**

- Labels used on more than one day: `Benign` (Friday-02-03-2018, Friday-16-02-2018, Friday-23-02-2018, Thuesday-20-02-2018, Thursday-01-03-2018, Thursday-15-02-2018, Thursday-22-02-2018, Wednesday-14-02-2018, Wednesday-21-02-2018, Wednesday-28-02-2018), `Infilteration` (Thursday-01-03-2018, Wednesday-28-02-2018), `Brute Force -Web` (Friday-23-02-2018, Thursday-22-02-2018), `Brute Force -XSS` (Friday-23-02-2018, Thursday-22-02-2018), `SQL Injection` (Friday-23-02-2018, Thursday-22-02-2018). No two label values differ only in case, spacing or punctuation, so each attack has one spelling across all files.
- Naming is not uniform: `DDOS attack-HOIC` / `DDOS attack-LOIC-UDP` versus `DDoS attacks-LOIC-HTTP`; `Infilteration` is misspelt; `Brute Force -Web` has an odd space. This is harmless for an exact mapping but must be copied exactly.
- **Missing attack:** the official schedule lists DDoS LOIC-UDP on 20-02, but the 20-02 file contains no LOIC-UDP label. LOIC-UDP appears in: Wednesday-21-02-2018 (1,730 flows). Heartbleed is described on the official page but has no label in any file.
- **Label noise:** in the first 200,000 rows of each file, groups of rows with identical features but different labels were found in Friday-23-02-2018 (4 groups), Thursday-01-03-2018 (5,020 groups), Thursday-22-02-2018 (3 groups). A follow-up check of the first 40 MB of the 01-03 file showed these groups mix `Benign` and `Infilteration`. Published work also reports labelling errors in this dataset (Liu et al., 2022).

## 6. Data quality (Verified)

Full-file checks cover every row for the listed columns; sample checks cover the first 200,000 rows of each file (1,999,980 rows in total) and are marked as such.

| Check | Scope | Count |
|---|---|---|
| Literal 'NaN' text in Flow Byts/s | full | 59,721 |
| 'Infinity' in Flow Byts/s | full | 36,039 |
| 'Infinity' in Flow Pkts/s | full | 95,760 |
| Negative Flow Duration | full | 14 |
| Negative Init Fwd Win Byts (-1 = not observed) | full | 4,432,608 |
| Repeated header lines inside data | full | 59 |
| Exact duplicate rows | sample | 230,497 |
| Duplicate rows if Timestamp is ignored | sample | 549,209 |
| Columns constant in every sample | sample | 8 |

- **Row-limit files:** 7 of 10 files have exactly 1,048,575 data lines (Friday-02-03-2018, Friday-16-02-2018, Friday-23-02-2018, Thursday-15-02-2018, Thursday-22-02-2018, Wednesday-14-02-2018, Wednesday-21-02-2018). This is Excel's maximum sheet size minus the header row. It strongly suggests these files passed through a spreadsheet and **may be truncated**. We could not confirm it from the times (next point); confirming it would need the raw PCAPs.
- **12-hour timestamps:** the latest time in any file is 12:59; no hour from 13 to 23 occurs, and there is no AM/PM marker. So morning and afternoon flows cannot be told apart, and the time order within a day is ambiguous. Some timestamps also fall outside the capture day (Thursday-22-02-2018, Wednesday-14-02-2018).
- **Protocols:** 0: 238,313, 17: 4,194,295, 6: 11,800,335 flows (6 = TCP, 17 = UDP, 0 = no transport protocol; in a checked sample all protocol-0 flows had destination port 0).
- **Constant columns** (no information in any sample): `Bwd Blk Rate Avg`, `Bwd Byts/b Avg`, `Bwd PSH Flags`, `Bwd Pkts/b Avg`, `Bwd URG Flags`, `Fwd Blk Rate Avg`, `Fwd Byts/b Avg`, `Fwd Pkts/b Avg`.
- **Duplicates** are very uneven by day. In the samples, 73% of rows in Wednesday-14-02-2018 and 40% in Friday-16-02-2018 are exact duplicates. Duplicates that end up on both sides of the train/test split inflate the scores.

## 7. Comparison with AIT (from H-1 evidence and this scan)

| Aspect | AIT Netflow (primary) | CSE-CIC-IDS2018 (backup) |
|---|---|---|
| Publisher / source | AIT Austrian Institute of Technology, Zenodo record 13168643 (2024) | CSE and Canadian Institute for Cybersecurity (UNB), public AWS bucket s3://cse-cic-ids2018 (2018) |
| Environment | 8 separate simulated small-company networks, 4-6 days each | 1 emulated organisation (420 machines, 30 servers, 50 attackers), 10 capture days |
| Files used | 8 ZIPs, 24 CSVs (Tstat), 273.7 MB compressed | 10 CSVs (CICFlowMeter-V3), 6.41 GiB uncompressed; raw PCAP/logs 446.3 GiB |
| Flows | 3,465,342 | 16,232,943 |
| Suspicious share | 17.86% | 16.93% |
| Columns | 138, 52, 28 (TCP complete / TCP non-complete / UDP) | 80 on 9 days; 84 on 1 day |
| Host identifiers (IP addresses) | Yes, in every file (client and server IP, host roles) | Only in 1 of 10 files (Thuesday-20-02-2018) |
| Timestamps | Epoch milliseconds plus full date-time | dd/mm/yyyy hh:mm:ss, hours only 01-12 (no AM/PM) |
| Labels | Official label_info.txt: 25 benign + 40 malicious labels, protocol-aware | 15 values in a single Label column; no official benign/malicious file |
| Attack types | One multi-step attack per network (scans, web attack, web shell, commands, DNS exfiltration) | Brute force, DoS, DDoS, web attacks, infiltration, botnet - one or two types per day |
| Binary mapping | Exact and official; 942 flows unmapped | Straightforward (Benign vs rest); 0 unmapped values |
| Main quality issues | 942 empty labels; placeholder text; 99% attacks in TCP non-complete | Inf/NaN text, negative values, repeated headers, row-limit files, 12-hour clock, label noise |
| Split by network (current plan) | Yes - 8 networks | No - only one network; split by day = split by attack type |
| Per-host 5-minute windows (H-4) | Possible | Only possible on 1 day; not on the others |
| Matching alert data for agents | AIT Alert Data Set from the same attacks | None provided by CIC |
| Processing in Colab | Easy (a few minutes) | Feasible by streaming in chunks (13 minutes for all 10 files) |

## 8. Fit with SentinelAI and the Random Forest

- **Random Forest: yes.** The 70+ numeric per-flow features are the kind of input a Random Forest handles well, and binary labels are easy to derive. After cleaning (Inf/NaN, constant columns, repeated headers) a flow-level model can be trained in Colab.
- **Planned host-window features (H-4): mostly no.** Connections, distinct ports and distinct hosts per host in a past-only 5-minute window need a source IP and a reliable time order. Only 1 of 10 files have IPs, and the 12-hour clock makes time order ambiguous.
- **Fair split (H-6): changes.** There is one network, not eight. Splitting by day means each test day has attack types the model never saw, which measures something different. A random split leaks near-duplicate flows.
- **Agents:** CIC provides no IDS alert set like the AIT Alert Data Set. The Investigation Agent would need synthetic or self-generated alerts. ATT&CK/Kill-Chain mappings would cover different techniques (brute force, DoS, botnet) than the AIT attack chain.

## 9. Backup decision

1. **Can it serve as a backup?** Yes, for the Random Forest detection part. It is official, public, labelled, and processable in Colab.
2. **Advantages over AIT:** many more flows and attack types (brute force, DoS/DDoS, web attacks, botnet, infiltration); widely used in published work, so results are easy to compare; a large attack share in several files.
3. **Disadvantages:** one network only (no split by network); IPs in only one file; 12-hour timestamps; files that may be truncated; Inf/NaN and negative values; repeated headers; duplicates; documented and observed label noise (especially infiltration); no matching alert data; no official binary label file.
4. **Modifications needed:** drop repeated header lines; replace or remove NaN/Infinity rows; treat -1 window values as 'not observed'; drop constant columns; remove exact duplicates before splitting; apply the exact label mapping above; consider excluding `Infilteration` or reporting results with and without it.
5. **Methodology changes if we switch:** feature module without per-host windows (or limited to the 20-02 file); a new split strategy (by day/attack type, or a deduplicated stratified split, stated clearly); retargeted rules (M-2) and ATT&CK subset (O-1); alerts for the agents generated from our own detections instead of AIT-ADS; updated proposal slides 8–11.

**Recommendation: Suitable with conditions.** Keep AIT as the primary dataset (H-1: conditional GO). Use CSE-CIC-IDS2018 (a) as the backup for the flow-level Random Forest if AIT fails, and (b) optionally as a second, out-of-distribution test set, as the proposal already allows. It is not a full replacement for the multi-agent part without extra work.

### How to switch if AIT fails the gate (tracker completion note)

1. Rerun `h2_ids2018_scan.py` to re-verify the 10 CSVs, and lock the label mapping (`ids2018_label_mapping.json`) in H-3.
2. Build a cleaning step: drop rows with Label = 'Label'; handle NaN/Infinity; drop constant columns; deduplicate.
3. Agree a new feature contract (ALL-1) based on per-flow CICFlowMeter features only, without IPs, ports used as identities, or timestamps.
4. Choose and document the split (by day / attack type, or a deduplicated stratified split) and update H-6.
5. Tell Malak (M-2/M-3), Reem (R-1/R-4) and Omar (O-1/O-3) which attack types and alert sources change.

## 10. Limitations of this verification

- Duplicate, conflict and constant-column checks used the first 200,000 rows of each file, not every row.
- Possible truncation was inferred from row counts; it was not confirmed against the raw PCAPs.
- S3 ETags were recorded, but CIC publishes no checksums for these files, so integrity can only be confirmed as 'complete download of the published bytes'.
- The binary mapping is proposed, not official. H-3 owns the final labelling rule.
- No model was trained; suitability for the Random Forest is judged from the features and labels, not from results.

## 11. Paragraph for the project documentation

As a backup to the AIT Netflow Data Set we verified CSE-CIC-IDS2018 (CSE and the Canadian Institute for Cybersecurity, 2018), using its official public AWS release. The ten processed CICFlowMeter CSV files (6.41 GiB, 16,232,943 labelled flows) were streamed in full. They contain 15 label values: 'Benign' and 14 attack labels covering brute force, DoS, DDoS, web attacks, infiltration and botnet traffic, giving 16.9% suspicious flows under our binary mapping. The data supports a flow-level Random Forest, but it comes from a single network. IP addresses are present on only one of ten days, and timestamps use a 12-hour clock without AM/PM, so our per-host time-window features and network-wise split cannot be reproduced. The files also need cleaning for Infinity/NaN values, repeated header lines, duplicates and known label noise. We therefore judge CSE-CIC-IDS2018 suitable, with conditions, as a backup for the detection model and as an optional second test set, while AIT remains the primary dataset.
